analysis.title: Dip buying lifts US stocks after tech sell-off (UBS House View - Daily US)
key_insights: US stocks rose sharply Monday (Nov 9) as investors returned to tech and growth shares after last week's sell-off. S&P 500 closed +2.4%, Nasdaq +2.7%. The rebound continued in Asia Tuesday, with AI-heavy indices in South Korea, Japan and Taiwan up 2% to 5%.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 6.9% and led the rebound. NVIDIA fell 4.3% after the start of an internal investigation into CEO Jensen Huang. Most S&P 500 sectors advanced, with consumer discretionary and communication services among the strongest. Airlines and cruise operators gained on lower expected fuel costs.

Oil extended its decline on possible progress in US-Iran diplomacy. Brent is down 8% this week to just below USD 90/bbl and WTI is near USD 84/bbl. Lower energy costs eased near-term inflation concerns ahead of Tuesday's US CPI report.

UBS reads the rebound as dip buying and a partial reversal of last week's sharp de-risking. It says the semiconductor and AI infrastructure decline was amplified by elevated positioning, high expectations and uncertainty over data center development. It calls the sell-off a positioning reset, not the start of a lasting downturn in the AI investment cycle.

UBS argues breadth supports its view. Last week's weakness was concentrated in chips, data center companies and other highly valued growth stocks, while Monday's gains covered most sectors. UBS reads this as investors differentiating between companies and parts of the AI ecosystem, not reassessing the growth and earnings outlook.

UBS says AI demand remains robust, citing accelerating cloud revenue and growing advance orders for computing capacity. Its AI capex forecast is USD 1.0tr in 2026, USD 1.4tr in 2027 and USD 1.5tr in 2028. It says political and physical constraints may delay, relocate or raise the cost of data center projects but are unlikely to eliminate demand.

Risks remain. Investors increasingly want evidence that AI spending generates sustainable revenue, utilization and returns. High expectations and concentrated positioning leave single companies sensitive to guidance, regulation, financing conditions and sentiment. UBS says further tech volatility would not be surprising.

Lower oil is a near-term tailwind for inflation, consumers and company costs. The physical oil market is still vulnerable after earlier supply disruptions and inventory drawdowns. Diplomatic progress could push prices lower, while renewed attacks or failed negotiations could quickly reverse the move.

Tuesday's US CPI report is the next test. Strong October employment data have kept expectations alive for a December Fed rate increase. A hotter reading could lift yields and challenge the equity rebound. Contained price pressure would support a measured tightening cycle.

UBS sees potential gains in broad equity indices over six to 12 months, backed by resilient earnings and growth. Its first recommendation is to manage concentration risk: keep AI exposure, but trim oversized single-name tech positions into strength. It favors established tech platforms with existing computing capacity, visible AI revenues, strong balance sheets and internal funding capacity.

UBS's second recommendation is to rebalance across sectors and regions. Preferred US sectors are industrials and health care. It prefers the Eurozone, where it expects 2027 earnings growth similar to the US at lower valuations.

UBS's third recommendation is to build a multi-asset core. Investors with large bond underweights should rebuild strategic allocations in high-quality short- and medium-term bonds. Alternatives and broad commodity exposure can add return and hedge geopolitical or inflation shocks.
